question: Research conducted in Italy on the engagement generated by content published on Meta over the past year has shown that content from recognised politicians is being systematically backdated without any explanation, while posts by influencers and members of the public containing hate speech and fake news is being suggested to users, making these more visible.

The Digital Services Act (DSA) lays down clear measures on shadow banning, which is effectively prohibited, while the Code of Practice on Disinformation and the Commission’s guidance published at the end of March contain clear recommendations on how to prevent the dissemination of hate speech and fake news.

The research seems to suggest that Meta, in order to avoid its responsibilities under the DSA, expressly hides political content because it is deemed potentially divisive, while it persists in promoting content generating engagement, even when this conveys dangerous messages.

These practices are particularly detrimental to politicians who are legitimately seeking to get their message across with the European elections approaching. With the entry into application of the DSA, the Commission has sent requests for information to Meta, including on shadow banning.
What answers has the Commission received from Meta and what further action does it intend to take, in view of the upcoming European elections, to severely curb these practices?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.5.2024) Regulation 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act – ‘DSA’)1 mentions ‘shadow banning’ (Recital 55) as a restriction of visibility that consists in demotion in ranking or in recommender systems, as well as in limiting accessibility by one or more recipients of the service or blocking the user from an online community without the user being aware.

The Commission has taken action within its supervisory powers under the DSA to investigate compliance with the DSA by a number of very large online platforms (‘VLOPs’). On 1 March 2024, the Commission sent a request for information (RFI) to Meta concerning, amongst other topics, shadow banning on Facebook and Instagram2.

On 30 April 2024, the Commission opened formal proceedings against Meta, including in relation to the policy linked to the ‘political content approach’, that demotes political content in the recommender systems.

The opening of proceedings is based on a preliminary analysis of the Meta’s risk assessment report, replies to the Commission’s formal RFI (which cannot be disclosed in full respect of the duty of professional secrecy3), publicly available reports and the Commission’s own analysis. All actions will be undertaken in full respect of due process, and we are currently not in a position to comment on the next steps.
Under the DSA, if at the end of an investigation, it is found that a provider has not complied, it can face a fine of up to 6% of its worldwide turnover.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single

Market for Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (OJ L 277, 27.10.2022). 2 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-sends-request-information-meta-under-digitalservices-act-1 3 Article 84 of the DSA.
